newsitem.title: UK: 1999 gilts still expensive on repo mkt, but less so.
newsitem.headline: 1999 gilts still expensive on repo mkt, but less so.

text.p: Three-year gilts continued to trade expensively in the repo market on Monday but not at the extraordinary levels seen on Friday, dealers said.
The 6.0 percent gilt due 1999 still traded down to three percent but that paled in comparison with Friday when some dealers said they had seen the stock bid at one percent.
Nonetheless, the three-year gilt continued to trade well below general collateral rates, which stood at about 5.85 percent.
"It's been trading around three percent, nothing like Friday but still well through GC," one repo trader said.
Other gilts also attracted moderately special status, although not as spectacularly as the three-year stock.
The trader said the 7.00 percent gilts of 2001 were trading 40 to 50 basis points through one-month GC, while the 6.0 percents of 2004 were also about 40 ticks under.
One-month GC was trading at 5.67/5.63 percent on Monday afternoon.
"The 7.25 (percents) of '98 are also picking up a bit of value now," the trader said. "They are about 15 basis points through."
Other than that, the market was quiet. "It is always like this ahead of a monetary meeting," the repo trader said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George meet for their monthly discussion of monetary policy on Wednesday.
A Reuter survey found 13 of 20 London-based economists did not expect Clarke to push through a rate cut this month.
"We're in the 50/50 camp but you get the feeling that official rates will stay at these levels for a while yet," one money market trader said.

The UK money market saw rates ease off on Monday. Having traded close to six percent on Friday, overnight unsecured rates dropped sharply but only after the Bank moved to take out the lion's share of a 750 million stg shortage at 1300 GMT.

"Everything was above 5-3/4 percent until the Bank moved in," the trader said. "Now you couldn't give money away at three percent. Cheap money has been coming too late in the day to be of any use to us."
"If anybody wanted cash now, the rates on the screen would be very different," he added.

The Bank of England did not operate in its early round on Monday, keeping money market rates firm. But in afternoon operations it bought bills worth 665 million stg and followed that up with 80 million stg of unspecified late assistance.
